To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the super-atom model is a real-space BCS model of high-TC superconductors.
the high-TC superconducting state is a resonant state of two Bose-Einsten condensates.
HTS is a real-space phenomenon that reflects cooperative co-existence, at the same TC, of two Bose-Einsteins condensates in real space, one a Cooper-pair condensate and a second, magnon condensates.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following topics: (i) Superconductivity in the cuprates.
the super-atom representation of high-Tc superconductivity.

a new approach to high-TC superconductors, which is based on the resonating-valence-bond RVB approach to superconductivity, and which leads to the conclusion that high-Tc superconductivity is a manifestation of a cooperative phenomenon involving the simultaneous formation of two Bose-Einsteins BE condensates, one of real-space Cooper pair BE condensate, the other of magnon BE condensate.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the super-atom representation of high-TC superconducting materials provides a new and powerful approach to understanding the nature of the high-TC phenomenon.
the superconducting state in the HTS materials, as well as in the BCS theory, can be understood in terms of a real-space condensation of Cooper pairs.
superconductivity is the result of a Bose-Einstein condensation of real-space Cooper-pairs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown how to make real space Cooper pairs and how to make HTS.
the super-exchange mechanism is a necessary, but not a sufficient condition to explain HTS.
we have demonstrated that the HTS is a Bose condensate of real-space Cooper pair and magnon excitations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the superconducting condensate in the electron-dopant HTS is formed by real-space Cooper pairs.
the real-space Cooper pair is not a conventional Cooper pair.
HTS is not a phenomenon that occurs at a critical temperature, but rather is an intrinsic property of the material.
